title: Dorothy Day (1897–1980)
hookLine: a journalist starts a newspaper and opens houses of hospitality in New York

lines: A NEW PAPER IN UNION SQUARE.
cards: Union Square, New York, in the hard years of the Depression. Street speakers on boxes, men out of work, pamphlets everywhere. A woman is selling a brand-new newspaper, cheap, with a plain title: The Catholic Worker.
She has written for radical papers for years. She has marched, been arrested, loved and lost, and become a Catholic, to the surprise of her old friends.
Now Dorothy Day wants a paper that tells workers the Church cares about them, and she is out in the square, selling it.

teach.b: First, the convert. Dorothy was a journalist and a socialist who knew the poor from the inside, from rented rooms and picket lines.
When her daughter Tamar was born, she was overwhelmed with gratitude, and she had the baby baptized, and then was baptized herself. It cost her the man she loved, who wanted no part of religion.
She wrote about that grief openly.

Second, the paper. With a French wanderer named Peter Maurin, who is tomorrow's story, she started The Catholic Worker. It took the Church's teaching on workers and the poor and put it on the street, in plain language.
Third, the house. People read the paper and came to the door hungry.
So she opened a house of hospitality: soup, coffee, a bed, a seat at the table, with no forms to fill in. Then another house, in other cities, and farms.

They called the whole movement by the paper's name, the Catholic Worker. The prophet Isaiah says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Deal thy bread to the hungry, and bring the needy and the harbourless into thy house."
Dorothy took it literally, day after day. Fourth, the title.
She wrote the story of her life and called it The Long Loneliness.

teach.h: DEAL THY BREAD TO THE HUNGRY.
teach.b: Her closing thought, in paraphrase: the answer to that loneliness is love, and love comes with community. Today the Church calls her a Servant of God, the first step toward sainthood.
She was wary of being called a saint, saying it made her too easy to dismiss.

how: Catholic Worker houses of hospitality still serve meals and offer beds in cities and on farms, run by volunteers who live simply and publish their own papers; Dorothy Day's cause for canonization is open.

games.q: your new paper tells readers the Church cares about the poor. hungry people start showing up at your door. what do you do?
o: send them to a city shelter.
open a house and feed them.
games.why: she opened a house of hospitality: soup, coffee, a bed, no forms. then more houses, and farms.

practice: Picture a table, any table: yours, a soup kitchen's, a desk at work.

Let one person come to mind who could use something to eat, a neighbor who lives alone, a coworker who skips lunch, someone you pass on the street, and think what one meal or one coffee would mean to them.
If you pray, pray for that person by name.

wordCard.voice: Catholic Worker. Dorothy Day's newspaper, and the movement of houses of hospitality that grew from it, feeding and housing whoever came to the door.

carryVoice: Your line: the long loneliness. A paper, a soup pot, and a door that stayed open. That's day nine hundred thirteen.
